text:
An approval screen is a starting point for verification.

CERT-In reports an AI-assisted campaign targeting Indian financial entities through their payment interfaces. Its earlier advisory describes stolen credentials enabling direct payment calls that bypass application checks.

My takeaway: a reassuring screen is insufficient evidence that authorization holds where money actually moves. If a transfer can bypass the checks behind that screen, the approval shown to a manager may tell only part of the story.

I’d make this concrete with one controlled test: trace a single approved payment from the decision through to the transfer. Ask the team to show what the final step checks against the approved recipient and amount, and what would stop a payment if those details changed.

One successful trace would not prove the whole system secure. It would give business and IT leaders something more useful than a reassuring display: evidence of whether the permission granted is the permission enforced.
